docs.title: TripEase
docs.text:
Author(s):

Nimitt Malhotra (1024030709), Manraj Singh (1024030712) and Vatsal Chauhan (1024030714)

TripEase is a web application for planning a trip in one place. Normally a group's plan is spread across a chat, a notes app, a maps app and a spreadsheet, and nobody knows which copy is the latest. In TripEase a trip is a single record that holds the itinerary, the places on a map and the budget together, and all of them update when the traveller edits the plan.

The project is at the mid-semester stage. The working prototype has sign-in, a new-trip wizard, city planning with an AI provider and a rule-based fallback, day-by-day itinerary generation, an editable roadmap, a map, feasibility checks and a budget with saving suggestions. The full list is in the README.

docs.title: Running the application
docs.text:
The application is in the code folder. You need Node.js 22 or newer.

cd code
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local     # then fill in the Firebase web configuration
npm run dev                    # http://localhost:3000

The full setup, including creating the Firebase project and the optional Google Places and Groq keys, is described in code/README.md.

docs.title: Activity Diagram
docs.text: This page has the activity diagram of the main use case, UC-2 Create a trip (see Use Cases). It shows what happens between the moment the traveller presses Generate my trip and the moment the new roadmap opens, and which part of the system does each step.

docs.title: 1. Notation
docs.text:
The notation is the one from the course slides on activity diagrams.

Symbol Meaning Filled circle Start. There is only one, with one transition leaving it. Circle with a ring around a filled centre End. There can be more than one. Long rounded rectangle An action. Arrow A transition. It shows the order of the actions. Large diamond with several exits A decision. Every exit carries a guard in square brackets, and together the guards cover all cases. Small empty diamond A merge. Several arrows enter it and one leaves. It is used instead of letting several arrows enter an action directly. Vertical columns (swimlanes) Who performs the action. Each action is placed in the lane of the part of the system that does it.

There are five lanes: the Traveller, TripEase (the browser and the API routes) and three outside systems, the AI provider, the Places provider and Cloud Firestore. The diagram has no fork and join, because all the actions are done one after another. The four place searches for a city do run at the same time in the code, but they are shown as one action.

docs.title: 3. Walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Validate the trip details. The wizard first calls POST /api/trips/plan. Every API route first checks the Firebase ID token of the signed-in user. The route then checks the trip details with a Zod schema and checks that the end date is not before the start date. If the check fails, the traveller sees an error and stays on the wizard.
  2. Ask the AI for a city split. TripEase asks the AI provider (Groq, or a mock provider when no key is set) how many days to spend in each city.
  3. Plan valid? The answer must pass the Zod schema and the constraint checks: the days add up to the length of the trip, no city is repeated, every city gets at least one day, there are at most 8 cities (and no more cities than days), and the plan is for the destination the traveller asked for.
  4. Retry allowed? If the plan is not valid, TripEase retries exactly once, and only when the error is something a model can fix: a plan that breaks a constraint, or an answer that is not valid JSON in the required shape. The second request carries a repair note that says what was wrong, and goes back to the AI through the merge before the request. Timeouts, authentication errors and quota errors are not retried. If there is no retry, or if the retry fails as well, TripEase uses the deterministic fallback planner. The same fallback is used when no AI provider is configured. The saved plan records whether it came from the AI or from the fallback.
  5. Re-check the plan on the server. The wizard then calls POST /api/trips/generate and sends the plan it received. A plan that arrives over the network is treated as client input, so the server checks it again and plans again if the check fails.
  6. Request places for every city. For each city, TripEase asks the places provider for one hotel, attractions, restaurants and nightlife. If a search fails or comes back empty, demo data is used for that search only, and every place is marked with its source.
  7. Build each day. Attractions are grouped into days by distance and visited nearest first. A stop is added to a day only if the day, travel time included, still fits in the 09:00 to 21:00 window, and time is held back for dinner. This uses the same arithmetic as the feasibility engine, so the generator does not create a day that the engine would then flag.
  8. Add a transfer. On the first day of every city except the first one, a transfer from the previous city is added as an estimated activity, with a travel mode (car, train or flight) chosen by distance.
  9. Work out the budget. The budget engine adds up the eight categories and compares the estimate with the budget the traveller entered. The savings suggestions are not made at this point. They are worked out when the trip page is shown.
  10. Save the trip. The server checks the generated itinerary against its schema and returns it. The browser then saves it as one document in Cloud Firestore, which only its owner can read or change, and opens the roadmap.

If any step after the first one fails (for example, the generated itinerary does not pass its schema), the wizard shows the error message and the traveller can try again. These error paths are left out of the diagram to keep it readable.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Data Model
docs.text: This page shows the data model of TripEase as an ER diagram in Chen notation. It describes the logical model: the things the app keeps track of and how they relate. How these are laid out in Firestore is explained in section 6.

docs.title: How to read the diagram
docs.text: Symbol Meaning Rectangle Entity Double rectangle Weak entity. It has no key of its own and is identified through the entity it belongs to. Diamond Relationship Double diamond Identifying relationship (the one that links a weak entity to its owner) Oval Attribute Underlined oval Key attribute Double oval Multivalued attribute (holds a list) Italic oval Composite attribute (made of several parts, listed in section 5) Double line Total participation: every instance of the entity takes part in the relationship 1 and N Cardinality at that end of the relationship

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text: Entities and relationships only, so the structure is easy to see.

docs.title: 2. With attributes
docs.text:
The same model with every attribute drawn. The image is large, so open it in a new tab to zoom in.

A few things that are not drawn as ovals:

  • ownerId on a trip is the foreign key behind the owns relationship, and cityId on a trip day is the foreign key behind hosts.
  • A trip's cities, days, budget and city plan are drawn as relationships, not as attributes.
  • dayCount on a trip and on a city can be worked out from the dates. We store it anyway because the roadmap and the budget use it all the time.

docs.title: 3. Entities
docs.text:
File paths in the last column are under code/src/.

Entity What it is Key Defined in User A traveller's account. Kept by Firebase Authentication, not in Firestore. uid lib/services/auth.ts Trip One planned trip: destination, dates, currency, who is travelling and their travel styles. id types/trip.ts City One city in a trip, with its dates, its position in the route and a search phrase for its photo. id types/itinerary.ts Hotel The hotel chosen for a city. Weak, because a hotel only exists as part of a city. none (identified by its city) types/itinerary.ts Trip Day One day of the trip. Points at the city where the day is spent. id types/itinerary.ts Activity One stop in a day: a sight, a meal, a nightlife spot or a transport step. id types/itinerary.ts Budget The budget breakdown of a trip. Weak, because there is exactly one per trip and it has no id. none (identified by its trip) types/budget.ts City Plan A record of how the cities were chosen: by the AI or by the fallback planner. Weak, for the same reason as Budget. none (identified by its trip) types/planning.ts

docs.title: 4. Relationships
docs.text:
Relationship Between Cardinality Participation How it is stored owns User and Trip 1 : N A trip must have an owner. A user may have no trips yet. ownerId on the trip. Firestore rules only let the owner read or change the trip. contains Trip and City 1 : N Both total. A trip has at least one city and a city belongs to one trip. The trip's cities list, ordered by order. has Trip and Trip Day 1 : N Both total. The trip's days list. hosts City and Trip Day 1 : N Both total. Every city gets at least one day. cityId on the day. stays at City and Hotel 1 : 1 Both total. The city's hotel field. includes Trip Day and Activity 1 : N An activity must belong to a day. A day can be empty. The day's activities list. has budget Trip and Budget 1 : 1 Both total. The trip's budget field. planned by Trip and City Plan 1 : 1 The plan must belong to a trip. A trip may have no plan: trips saved before the planner existed do not have one. The trip's optional planning field.

The has relationship is partly redundant. A day already points to its city, and the city to its trip, so the trip of a day could be found that way. We draw it anyway because the days are stored directly under the trip, and the trip page reads them from there.

docs.title: 5. Composite and multivalued attributes
docs.text:
Entity Attribute Kind Parts Trip preferences Multivalued One or more travel styles: beaches, food, culture, adventure, nightlife, shopping, nature, relaxation Budget categories Composite Eight amounts: flights, hotels, food, activities, transport, shopping, misc, buffer City Plan allocations Composite and multivalued A list with one entry per city, each with a city name, a number of days and a short reason Hotel, Activity location Composite lat, lng Hotel, Activity rating Composite value, count Hotel, Activity source Composite provider (mock or google), providerPlaceId, sourceUrl, sourceName

Values that are limited to a fixed set:

  • Trip status is generating or ready.
  • Trip travelerType is solo, couple, family, friends or custom.
  • Activity category is one of sightseeing, food, adventure, beach, culture, relaxation, shopping, nightlife or transport.
  • City Plan source is ai or fallback.

Optional attributes: on Hotel and Activity, location, address, rating, imageUrl, source and priceIsEstimate can be missing. Older trips do not have them, and neither do activities the user adds by hand. referenceUrl can be empty, and fallbackReason on a city plan is only filled when the AI plan was not used. A place with no real source is shown as "Demo data" (FR-12).

docs.title: 6. How it is stored
docs.text:
The model above is the logical view. In Firestore a whole trip is one document, trips/{tripId}, and everything that belongs to it sits inside that document: the cities (each with its hotel), the days (each with its activities), the budget and the city plan. We did it this way because a trip is small, with a handful of cities and a couple of dozen activities, so it stays well below Firestore's 1 MiB document limit, and the page loads and saves in a single read or write. The cost is that when the user edits one activity, the whole days list and the budget are written back, not just that activity. That is fine at this size.

The user is not in Firestore at all. The account lives in Firebase Authentication, and a trip refers to it through ownerId.

Some things in the code are not in the diagram because they are worked out when needed and never saved: travel segments between stops, the feasibility result for a day, savings suggestions, and the places returned by the places provider (these are turned into activities and hotels when an itinerary is built).

The security rules also mention a users collection and itineraryItems and expenses subcollections under a trip. The rules and their tests cover them, but the app does not read or write them yet, so they are left out of the diagram.

docs.title: DFD Level 0 (Context Diagram)
docs.text: TripEase is shown as a single process with its external entities: the traveller, Firebase Authentication, the places provider, the AI provider and the OpenStreetMap tile server.

docs.title: DFD Level 1
docs.text:
Notation: a circle is a process, a rounded rectangle is an external entity, and a name between two parallel lines is a data store.

  • 1.0 Authenticate User: the traveller signs in through Firebase Authentication, which returns an ID token. The API routes for planning, generation, rebuilding and place search verify this token on every request. The photo route uses signed links instead, because an image request cannot carry the token.
  • 2.0 Plan Cities: Groq AI suggests how many days to spend in each city. The suggestion is validated, and a deterministic fallback planner is used if it is missing or invalid.
  • 3.0 Generate Itinerary: places are fetched from Google Places and arranged into days. Feasibility checks decide whether an activity fits in a day, and the budget is calculated. It also rebuilds the itinerary when the city list is edited.
  • 4.0 Manage Trip: saves the trip record to D1 and handles edits, renaming, deletion and replacing a place (which searches Google Places). The budget is recalculated after every edit.
  • 5.0 Analyse Feasibility: reads the trip record and works out travel time between stops and days that are too full.
  • 6.0 Show Roadmap, Map and Budget: shows the roadmap with place photos, the map with OpenStreetMap tiles, the budget breakdown, savings suggestions and feasibility warnings.

D1 Trips: one Firestore document per trip, readable and writable only by its owner (enforced by Firestore security rules).

When no Google Places or Groq key is configured, the system uses built-in demo providers instead. These are internal to the system, so they are not shown as external entities.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: This page has the requirements for TripEase as of the mid-semester evaluation. We follow the classification from the course: functional requirements, non-functional requirements (product, organisational and external) and domain requirements. Every requirement has an ID so we can refer to it in the report. "Shall" marks a mandatory requirement. "Done" means it works in the current build and "Planned" means we are doing it before the final submission.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
TripEase is meant to replace the usual mix of WhatsApp chats, notes, Google Maps and a spreadsheet that people use to plan a trip. The itinerary, the map and the budget are all part of one trip, so when you change one the others update too.

What it does not do: it does not book anything and it does not show live prices. All costs in the app are estimates.

One thing changed from the proposal. In the proposal we kept AI-generated itineraries out of scope. In iteration 4 we ended up using an AI model for one small part, which is deciding how many days to spend in each city. It does not pick places or prices. We check its answer with our own rules, and if the AI is down or gives a bad answer we use a normal (non-AI) planner instead. So the app still works without it.

docs.title: 2. Who and what uses the system
docs.text: Actor Role Traveller The user. Makes trips, edits them, looks at the map and budget. Has to be signed in for everything except the landing page. Firebase Authentication Sign-up and sign-in (email/password or Google). Cloud Firestore Where users and trips are stored. Places provider Gives us hotels, sights, restaurants and nightlife. Google Places, or our demo data if there is no key. AI provider Suggests the city split. Groq, or a mock for testing. OpenStreetMap Map tiles.

docs.title: 3. Functional requirements
docs.text: These say what the system does, how it reacts to inputs and how it behaves in different situations.

Done FR-5 If a user starts a trip on the landing page and then signs up, the system shall keep what they entered. Done

docs.title: 4. Non-functional requirements
docs.text: These are constraints on how the system works. We have grouped them the way the course does: product, organisational and external. Where we could, we wrote them so they can be tested.

docs.title: 4.1 Product requirements
docs.text: ID Type Requirement How we check it Status NFR-1 Reliability The app shall work end to end with no Google Places or Groq key, using demo data. If a Google Places search fails or comes back empty, the gap shall be filled with demo data instead of failing the whole trip. Run the app with no keys set. Done NFR-2 Reliability Sign-in and saving a trip shall be available at least 99% of the time on staging during the pilot. Uptime during the pilot window. Planned NFR-3 Efficiency (performance) A call to the AI shall time out after 20 seconds, after which the non-AI planner shall be used. Groq provider tests (timeout case) and planning pipeline tests (fallback). Done NFR-4 Efficiency (performance) Place searches shall be cached on the server for 10 minutes (500 entries at most), so the same search is not paid for twice. Cache unit tests. Done NFR-5 Usability A first-time user shall be able to finish a 3-day trip with at least 5 stops in 15 minutes or less (median). This is the TTCI target from the proposal. Pilot study, 12 to 20 participants. Planned NFR-6 Usability The layout shall adapt to phone and laptop screens, and both light and dark themes shall be supported. Check by hand in a narrow window. Done NFR-7 Security Only the owner of a trip shall be able to read, edit or delete it, and the owner shall not be changeable after the trip is created. Everything else is denied by default (Firestore security rules). Security rules tests on the emulator, run in CI. Done NFR-8 Security The routes for planning, generation, rebuilding and place search shall need a valid Firebase login token. The photo route shall accept only signed URLs. A request without a token gets 401 (403 for photos); token checks have unit tests. Done NFR-9 Security The Google Places and Groq keys shall be read only on the server and never sent to the browser. Keys have no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix. Done NFR-10 Maintainability Places and AI shall sit behind interfaces, and all database access shall go through service files, so a provider can be switched without changing the rest of the code. Code review. Done NFR-11 Data limits Destination shall be 2 to 80 characters, budget more than 0 and at most 100,000,000, travellers 1 to 20, travel styles 1 to 8, currency one of INR, USD, EUR or GBP, the end date shall not be before the start date, and a trip shall have at most 8 cities. Zod schemas in the API routes, the wizard's date check, and the plan checks (FR-9). Done

docs.title: 4.2 Organisational requirements
docs.text: ID Type Requirement Status NFR-12 Implementation The app shall be built with Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Firebase for login and storage and no separate backend server. Server-side work shall be done in Next.js API routes. Done NFR-13 Standards (process) Every push shall run lint, unit tests, the security rules tests and a production build on GitHub Actions. Work shall be done on separate branches and merged into main. Done NFR-14 Delivery Every merge into main shall be deployed automatically to a staging site on Vercel. Done

docs.title: 4.3 External requirements
docs.text: ID Type Requirement Status NFR-15 Interoperability The map shall use OpenStreetMap tiles with the attribution their usage policy asks for, and places shall be fetched through the provider interface so Google Places can be used when a key is given. Done NFR-16 Ethical Travel times, distances and costs shall always be labelled as estimates, and a place shall never be shown as verified unless it has a real source. Done NFR-17 Privacy A trip shall be visible only to its owner. The pilot shall not collect location history or contact details, and participants shall be told what is recorded. Done (trips) / Planned (pilot)

docs.title: 5. Domain requirements
docs.text:
These come from the travel and budgeting domain. If they are wrong, the output looks wrong to anyone who has planned a trip.

ID Requirement DR-1 A sightseeing day shall be measured against a 09:00 to 21:00 window. Time at places, travel between them and a buffer for queues all count towards it. DR-2 The budget shall add a small fixed daily allowance (500) for local transport, a miscellaneous amount of 4% of the other costs, and a buffer of 5% of the user's budget, with a minimum of 3000. DR-3 The trip shall be priced for the whole group. Flights shall be multiplied by the number of travellers, and the other costs are for the group as a whole. DR-4 The stops in a day shall be visited nearest-first starting from the hotel, so the day does not zigzag across the city. DR-5 A change of city shall appear as its own travel step on the arrival day, with a mode and a duration.

docs.title: UC-1: Sign up / sign in
docs.text:
Actors: Traveller, Firebase Authentication

  1. The user opens sign-in or sign-up.
  2. They enter email and password, or pick Google.
  3. Firebase checks it and gives back a token.
  4. They land on the dashboard.

If the details are wrong, an error is shown and they stay on the same page.

docs.title: UC-2: Create a trip
docs.text:
Actors: Traveller, AI provider, places provider. The user must be signed in.

  1. The user goes through the wizard.
  2. The app asks the AI how to split the days between cities.
  3. The split is checked against FR-9.
  4. Places are fetched for each city and the days are filled in, checking that each day fits.
  5. The budget is worked out and the trip is saved.
  6. The trip page opens with the roadmap, map and budget.

If the AI fails at step 2 or 3, the non-AI planner makes the split and the loading screen tells the user.

docs.title: UC-3: Edit the itinerary
docs.text:
Actor: Traveller (owner of the trip)

  1. The user adds, edits, removes or drags an activity, or changes a hotel.
  2. The change is saved.
  3. The budget, warnings and map update.

docs.title: UC-4: Edit cities
docs.text:
Actors: Traveller, places provider

  1. The user opens "Edit cities" and makes changes.
  2. The days are rebalanced and FR-9 is checked.
  3. The server checks it again and only rebuilds the cities that are new or changed. Cities that weren't touched keep their activities.

If a rule is broken, the problem is shown and nothing is saved.

docs.title: UC-5: Replace a place
docs.text:
Actors: Traveller, places provider

  1. From an activity, the user searches for a place.
  2. Matching places come back from the provider.
  3. The user picks one and it replaces the activity.

If the live search fails, demo results are shown with a message saying so.

docs.title: UC-6: View map and budget
docs.text:
Actors: Traveller, OpenStreetMap

  1. The user opens the map or budget tab.
  2. The map shows the places and the day lines, for the whole trip, a city or a day.
  3. The budget tab shows each category, and savings tips if the trip is over budget.

docs.title: UC-7: Manage trips
docs.text:
Actor: Traveller

  1. The user opens the dashboard and sees their trips.
  2. They open one, or delete one from its card.
  3. On the trip page they can rename it.

docs.title: 7. Assumptions and limits of the current build
docs.text:
• Travel times are worked out from distance, not from a routing service. We don't fetch opening hours either.
  • Google Places charges per request, which is why it is optional and the results are cached.
  • The Google Places provider is written against the documented API but we have not tested it with a live key yet. All our tests use the demo provider.
  • The 3000 minimum buffer and the 500 daily transport allowance are fixed numbers in the code. They are not converted when the trip is in USD, EUR or GBP, so they are too big for those currencies.
  • A Firebase login token that has been revoked still works until it expires (up to an hour), because we check tokens against Google's public keys and not with the Firebase Admin SDK.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: This page has the use case diagram of TripEase and a description of every use case, written with the use case template from the course. UC-1 to UC-7 are the use cases from the requirements page. UC-8 to UC-12 are supporting use cases that the main ones include or extend. FR-25 to FR-27 are still planned, so they have no use cases yet.

docs.title: 1. Actors
docs.text:
Actor Category What it does Traveller Primary actor Uses the main functions of the system: creates trips, edits them, looks at the map and the budget. Firebase Authentication Other system Signs the traveller up and in, with email and password or with Google. Cloud Firestore Other system Stores the trips. Only the owner of a trip can read or change it. AI provider (Groq, or a mock for testing) Other system Suggests how many days to spend in each city. Places provider (Google Places, or our demo data) Other system Gives us hotels, sights, restaurants and nightlife. OpenStreetMap Other system Gives the map tiles.

We have no secondary actor, because the app has no admin role, and no external hardware.

docs.title: 2. Diagram
docs.text: The notation is the one from the course slides. A stick figure is an actor and sits outside the system boundary, an oval is a use case, and a plain line joins an actor to the use cases it takes part in. A dashed arrow marked <<includes>> points to the use case that is included. A dashed arrow marked <<extends>> points to the use case that is extended. We kept the spelling used in the slides.

docs.title: Relationships between use cases
docs.text:
Use case Relationship Use case Why UC-2 Create a trip includes UC-8 Plan city split Every new trip needs its cities decided first. UC-2 Create a trip includes UC-10 Fetch places The days are filled with real places. UC-2 Create a trip includes UC-11 Work out budget and save trip A new trip gets a budget and is saved. UC-3 Edit the itinerary includes UC-11 Work out budget and save trip Every edit changes the budget and has to be saved. UC-4 Edit cities includes UC-10 Fetch places A new city needs places. UC-4 Edit cities includes UC-11 Work out budget and save trip The rebuilt trip gets a new budget and is saved. UC-5 Replace a place includes UC-10 Fetch places The search for a place goes to the places provider. UC-9 Use fallback planner extends UC-8 Plan city split Only used when the AI is not available or its plan is not accepted. UC-5 Replace a place extends UC-3 Edit the itinerary Only used when the traveller searches for a real place while editing an activity. UC-12 Show savings suggestions extends UC-6 View map and budget Only used when the trip is over budget.

Two more notes on what the diagram leaves out. Every use case except UC-1 needs a signed-in traveller, and we did not draw an include arrow for that, to keep the diagram readable. It is a pre condition in each template below. Signing out (FR-3) is a single action, so it is not drawn as a use case. There is no generalisation, because there is only one kind of human actor.

docs.title: 3. Use case descriptions
docs.text: In the flows, AA is an actor action, SR is a system response and SA is a system action.

docs.title: UC-1: Sign up / sign in
docs.text:
Use case UC-1 Sign up / sign in Actors Traveller (initiates), Firebase Authentication Type Primary Purpose Let a traveller into the app with an account. Overview The traveller creates an account or signs in, with email and password or with Google. Pre condition The traveller is not signed in. Post condition The traveller is signed in and can open the dashboard and the trip pages. Requirements FR-1, FR-2, FR-4, FR-5

Typical course of events

  1. (AA) The traveller opens the sign-in page. A new traveller opens the sign-up page instead.
  2. (SR) The system shows a form with email, password (at least 6 characters) and, on sign-up, an optional name. There is also a "Continue with Google" button.
  3. (AA) The traveller enters the email and password and submits the form.
  4. (SA) The system passes the details to Firebase Authentication, to sign in or to create the account.
  5. (AA) Firebase Authentication accepts the details and signs the traveller in.
  6. (SR) The system opens the trip wizard if the traveller had started a trip on the landing page. Otherwise it opens the dashboard.

Alternate flow

  • Step 1: The traveller was sent here because they opened the dashboard or a trip page without being signed in.
  • Step 3: The traveller chooses "Continue with Google" and finishes in the Google pop-up. The flow continues at step 5.

Exceptional flow

  • Step 5: Firebase Authentication refuses (wrong email or password, an account that already exists, a weak password, too many attempts, a network problem), or the Google window is closed. The system shows a message and the traveller stays on the same page.

docs.title: UC-2: Create a trip
docs.text:
Use case UC-2 Create a trip Actors Traveller (initiates). The AI provider, the places provider and Cloud Firestore take part through UC-8, UC-10 and UC-11. Type Primary Purpose Turn a few answers into a full trip with cities, days, hotels, activities and a budget. Overview The traveller goes through the wizard. The system decides the cities, fills the days with places, works out the budget and saves the trip. Pre condition The traveller is signed in. Post condition The trip is saved under the traveller's account and its page is open. Includes UC-8 Plan city split, UC-10 Fetch places, UC-11 Work out budget and save trip Requirements FR-5 to FR-12, FR-23

Typical course of events

  1. (AA) The traveller selects "Create new trip" on the dashboard, or arrives from the landing page after signing up.
  2. (SR) The system opens the wizard. If the traveller started a trip on the landing page, destination, dates, budget and currency are already filled in.
  3. (AA) The traveller goes through the steps: destination, dates, budget and currency, travellers, travel style, and a final review.
  4. (SR) The system lets the traveller go to the next step only when the current one is valid.
  5. (AA) The traveller selects "Generate my trip".
  6. (SA) The system decides the cities (UC-8). The loading screen shows the cities it chose.
  7. (SA) The system fetches places for each city (UC-10), arranges them into days and checks the result.
  8. (SA) The system works out the budget and saves the trip (UC-11).
  9. (SR) The trip page opens with the roadmap, the map and the budget.

Alternate flow

  • Step 2: There is no landing-page draft, so the wizard starts with default values.
  • Step 3: The traveller goes back to a previous step and changes an answer.

Exceptional flow

  • Step 4: The destination is shorter than 2 characters, the end date is before the start date, the budget is not above 0, or there are no travellers. The "Next" button stays disabled.
  • Steps 6 to 8: A service fails, the session has expired, or the server rejects the details (for example, no travel style was chosen). The wizard shows the error message and goes back to the review step with the answers still filled in.

docs.title: UC-3: Edit the itinerary
docs.text:
Use case UC-3 Edit the itinerary Actors Traveller (initiates). Cloud Firestore takes part through UC-11. Type Primary Purpose Let the traveller change the plan to what they actually want. Overview The traveller adds, edits, removes or reorders activities, or changes the hotel of a city. The budget, the warnings and the map follow the change. Pre condition The traveller is signed in, owns the trip and has the trip page open. Post condition The change is saved and the budget matches the new plan. Includes UC-11 Work out budget and save trip Extended by UC-5 Replace a place Requirements FR-15, FR-16, FR-18, FR-22, FR-23

Typical course of events

  1. (AA) The traveller adds an activity to a day, edits or removes one, drags an activity to a new position, or changes the hotel of a city.
  2. (SR) For an added or edited activity, or for a hotel change, the system opens a form with the details.
  3. (AA) The traveller fills in the form and saves it.
  4. (SA) The system works out the new budget and saves the change (UC-11).
  5. (SR) The roadmap, the map, the budget and the warnings for each day update.

Alternate flow

  • Step 1: Removing or dragging an activity needs no form, so the flow goes straight to step 4.
  • Step 2: While the form is open, the traveller can search for a real place (UC-5).

Exceptional flow

  • Step 3: In the activity form, the name is empty or the reference link is not a full URL. The form shows a message, stays open and nothing is saved.

docs.title: UC-4: Edit cities
docs.text:
Use case UC-4 Edit cities Actors Traveller (initiates). The places provider and Cloud Firestore take part through UC-10 and UC-11. Type Primary Purpose Let the traveller change which cities are visited and for how many days. Overview The traveller adds, removes, renames or re-times cities. The system checks the new list and rebuilds only the cities that are new or changed. Pre condition The traveller is signed in, owns the trip and has the trip page open. Post condition The trip has the new cities and days, a new budget and the updated plan. Cities that were not touched keep their activities. Includes UC-10 Fetch places, UC-11 Work out budget and save trip Requirements FR-9, FR-17

Typical course of events

  1. (AA) The traveller selects "Edit cities" on the roadmap.
  2. (SR) The system shows the cities with their number of days.
  3. (AA) The traveller adds a city, removes one, renames one or changes its days.
  4. (SR) The system checks the list while the traveller types. The days must add up to the length of the trip, no city can be repeated, every city needs at least 1 day, there can be at most 8 cities, and no more cities than days.
  5. (AA) The traveller saves the list.
  6. (SA) The server checks the list again and rebuilds the trip. Cities that were not changed keep their activities, and new cities get places from the places provider (UC-10).
  7. (SA) The system works out the budget and saves the trip, together with a note that the cities were edited by the traveller (UC-11).
  8. (SR) The roadmap, the map and the budget show the new cities.

Alternate flow

  • Step 3: The last remaining city cannot be removed, and a city cannot be added once there are as many cities as days. Those buttons are disabled.

Exceptional flow

  • Step 4: The list breaks one of the rules. The system shows the first problem, the "Save" button is disabled and nothing is saved.
  • Steps 6 and 7: The server refuses the list or something fails. The dialog shows the error and the trip stays as it was.

docs.title: UC-5: Replace a place
docs.text:
Use case UC-5 Replace a place Actors Traveller (initiates). The places provider takes part through UC-10. Type Primary Purpose Let the traveller swap an activity for a real place, so that its location and source stay attached. Overview In the activity form, the traveller searches for a place, picks one, and the form is filled with its details. Pre condition The traveller is signed in and has the add or edit activity form open (UC-3). Post condition The activity refers to the chosen place and keeps its location and source. Includes UC-10 Fetch places Extends UC-3 Edit the itinerary Requirements FR-12, FR-16

Typical course of events

  1. (AA) The traveller types at least 2 characters in "Replace with a real place" and starts the search.
  2. (SA) The system asks the places provider (UC-10) for matching places in the destination of the trip. It looks for restaurants if the activity is a food activity and for attractions otherwise.
  3. (SR) The system lists the matches with name, rating, address, coordinates and estimated price. Demo places are marked "Demo".
  4. (AA) The traveller picks a place.
  5. (SR) The system fills the form with the name, category, description, duration, estimated cost and source link of the place, and keeps its location and source attached.
  6. (AA) The traveller saves the form. The flow continues at step 4 of UC-3.

Alternate flow

  • Step 4: No place matched. The system suggests a broader search or typing the name by hand.
  • Step 5: The traveller types over the name after picking a place. The place is detached, so the activity has no location or source any more.

Exceptional flow

  • Step 2: The live provider fails. The system shows demo places and a notice that says so.
  • Step 2: The search cannot be done at all (for example a network error or an expired session). The form shows a message and the traveller can still type a name.

docs.title: UC-6: View map and budget
docs.text:
Use case UC-6 View map and budget Actors Traveller (initiates), OpenStreetMap, Cloud Firestore Type Primary Purpose Show the plan on a map and show what it costs. Overview The traveller opens a trip and looks at the roadmap with the map beside it, then at the budget. Pre condition The traveller is signed in and owns the trip. Post condition None. This use case only reads the trip. Extended by UC-12 Show savings suggestions Requirements FR-19 to FR-23

Typical course of events

  1. (AA) The traveller opens a trip from the dashboard.
  2. (SA) The system loads the trip from Cloud Firestore and keeps listening for changes.
  3. (SR) The Roadmap tab shows the cities and days with the estimated travel time between stops. A day that does not fit between 09:00 and 21:00 is marked red, and a tight day amber. The map is next to it.
  4. (AA) The traveller sets the map to the whole trip, a city or a day, or selects a pin or a place in the roadmap.
  5. (SR) The map shows the matching pins on OpenStreetMap tiles. For a day it joins the stops in order with a line, and for the whole trip it joins the cities. Selecting a pin opens the place in the roadmap and the other way round.
  6. (AA) The traveller opens the Budget tab.
  7. (SR) The system shows the budget, the estimated cost, how much is left or over, and the cost of each category: hotels, flights, food, activities, transport, shopping, miscellaneous and emergency buffer.

If the estimate is above the budget, UC-12 adds its suggestions after step 7.

Alternate flow

  • Step 3: On a small screen the traveller shows or hides the map with a button.

Exceptional flow

  • Step 2: The trip cannot be loaded. The page shows a message. If the trip does not exist or is not the traveller's, the page says so and links back to the dashboard.
  • Step 5: A place without coordinates is not on the map. The map says how many places are missing.

docs.title: UC-7: Manage trips
docs.text:
Use case UC-7 Manage trips Actors Traveller (initiates), Cloud Firestore Type Primary Purpose Let the traveller find, open, rename and delete their trips. Overview The dashboard lists the traveller's own trips. From there a trip can be opened or deleted, and on the trip page it can be renamed. Pre condition The traveller is signed in. Post condition The dashboard and the trip page show the current trips and titles. Requirements FR-13, FR-14

Typical course of events

  1. (AA) The traveller opens the dashboard.
  2. (SA) The system loads the traveller's trips from Cloud Firestore and keeps listening for changes.
  3. (SR) The system shows each trip as a card with its title, dates, number of travellers and budget. Trips that have not ended yet are under "Your trips" and finished ones under "Past trips".
  4. (AA) The traveller opens a trip.
  5. (SR) The trip page opens (UC-6).

Alternate flow

  • Step 4: Delete: the traveller selects the bin icon on a card and the card asks for confirmation. On "Confirm" the system deletes the trip from Cloud Firestore and the card disappears. On "Cancel" nothing happens.
  • Step 4: Rename: on the trip page the traveller selects the pencil next to the title, types a new title and saves. The system stores the new title. An empty title is not saved.
  • Step 3: The traveller has no trips yet. The system shows an empty page with a button to create the first trip (UC-2).

Exceptional flow

  • Step 2: The trips cannot be loaded. The dashboard shows a message.
  • Step 4: A delete fails. The card shows the error and the trip stays.

docs.title: UC-8: Plan city split
docs.text:
Use case UC-8 Plan city split Actors AI provider. The system starts it as part of UC-2. Type Secondary Purpose Decide which cities to visit and how many days to spend in each. Overview The AI provider suggests a split and the system accepts it only if it passes our own checks. The AI does not pick places or prices. Pre condition The traveller has finished the wizard. Post condition The system has a valid city plan, whatever the AI did. Extended by UC-9 Use fallback planner Requirements FR-8, FR-9, FR-10

Typical course of events

  1. (SA) The system sends the trip details (destination, dates, number of days, travellers, budget, currency and travel styles) to the AI provider and asks for a split of the days between cities.
  2. (AA) The AI provider answers with a list of cities, the days for each one and a short reason.
  3. (SA) The system checks the answer. It must be for the same destination, the days must add up to the length of the trip, no city can be repeated, every city needs at least 1 day, there can be at most 8 cities, and no more cities than days.
  4. (SR) The plan is accepted and recorded together with the planner that made it. The loading screen shows the cities and marks the route as AI planned.

Alternate flow

  • Step 3: The answer is not valid JSON in the expected shape, or it fails the checks. The system asks the AI provider once more and tells it what was wrong.

Exceptional flow

  • Steps 1 to 3: There is no AI key, the provider fails, it takes longer than 20 seconds, or the second answer is still not valid. The system goes to UC-9.

docs.title: UC-9: Use fallback planner
docs.text:
Use case UC-9 Use fallback planner Actors None. This is done by the system alone. Type Secondary Purpose Make sure a trip can always be planned, even without the AI. Overview The system splits the days between cities with its own rules. Pre condition The AI is not available, or its plan was not accepted in UC-8. Post condition A valid city plan, recorded as "fallback" with the reason. Extends UC-8 Plan city split Requirements FR-10

Typical course of events

  1. (SA) The system splits the days between cities for the destination, using its own planner.
  2. (SA) The system runs the same checks as in step 3 of UC-8.
  3. (SA) The system records the plan as "fallback", with the reason.
  4. (SR) The loading screen marks the route as planned by TripEase and says that AI planning is not available right now. It is not shown as an error.

docs.title: UC-10: Fetch places
docs.text:
Use case UC-10 Fetch places Actors Places provider. The system starts it as part of UC-2, UC-4 or UC-5. Type Secondary Purpose Get real places for a trip. Overview The system asks the places provider for hotels, sights, restaurants and nightlife of a city, or for the words the traveller searched for. Pre condition The caller has a destination and what to look for. Post condition The caller has a list of places that each say where they came from. Requirements FR-11, FR-12

Typical course of events

  1. (SA) The system asks the places provider for places in a city, or for the search words of the traveller.
  2. (AA) The places provider returns places with name, location, rating, estimated price, photo link and source.
  3. (SA) The system keeps answers from the live provider for 10 minutes (at most 500 entries), so the same search is not paid for twice.
  4. (SR) The places go back to the caller.

Exceptional flow

  • Step 2: There is no Google key, the live search fails or it finds nothing. The system uses demo places instead. They are marked "Demo data".

docs.title: UC-11: Work out budget and save trip
docs.text:
Use case UC-11 Work out budget and save trip Actors Cloud Firestore. The system starts it as part of UC-2, UC-3 and UC-4. Type Secondary Purpose Keep the budget and the saved trip in line with the plan. Overview After a trip is built or changed, the system works out the budget and writes the trip to Cloud Firestore. Pre condition A trip was built or changed. Post condition The stored trip and its budget agree with each other. Requirements FR-18, FR-23

Typical course of events

  1. (SA) The system works out the budget from the cities, the days, the activities and the number of travellers: hotels, flights, food, activities, transport, shopping, miscellaneous and the emergency buffer, and the total estimate.
  2. (SA) The system writes the changed parts of the trip to its document in Cloud Firestore (a new trip is created with the traveller as owner) and updates the time of the last change.
  3. (AA) Cloud Firestore accepts the write if the traveller is signed in and owns the trip.

Exceptional flow

  • Step 3: Cloud Firestore refuses the write because the traveller is not signed in or does not own the trip. Nothing is saved.

docs.title: UC-12: Show savings suggestions
docs.text:
Use case UC-12 Show savings suggestions Actors Traveller (initiates) Type Secondary Purpose Help the traveller bring an over-budget trip back within budget. Overview When the estimate is above the budget, the Budget tab lists up to three ways to save and the traveller can apply one. Pre condition The Budget tab is open and the estimated total is above the budget. Post condition If a suggestion was applied, the trip and its budget are changed and saved. Extends UC-6 View map and budget Requirements FR-24

Typical course of events

  1. (SR) The system shows a warning with the amount by which the trip is over budget.
  2. (SR) The system lists up to three ways to save, each with the estimated saving: a more modest hotel in the city with the priciest hotel, a shared tour instead of the most expensive non-food activity, and local restaurants instead of hotel dining.
  3. (AA) The traveller selects "Apply" on one of them.
  4. (SA) The system changes the trip. The hotel is replaced by a budget option at 70% of the nightly price and marked as demo data, the activity becomes a shared tour at 40% of its cost, or the food costs go down by 15%. The system then works out the budget again and saves the trip.
  5. (SR) The Budget tab shows the new numbers.

Alternate flow

  • Step 3: The traveller ignores the suggestions and leaves the trip as it is.

docs.title: 4. Regenerating the image
docs.text:
The .dot source and the stick figure it uses (actor.png) are in docs/diagrams/. The positions are set by hand in the file, so the layout stays the same. From that folder:

neato -n -Tpng -Gdpi=80 usecase.dot -o usecase.png

docs.title: Week 1 : Requirements that Did Not Match the Proposal, and the Data Model
Problem
docs.text: I had to write the requirements document for TripEase. While doing it I found that it could not simply repeat the project proposal. The proposal kept AI-generated itineraries out of scope, but the code we had built already used an AI model for one small decision: how many days to spend in each city.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The course asks for requirements in four groups: functional requirements, non-functional requirements (split into product, organisational and external) and domain requirements. Every requirement needs an ID so that it can be traced to a use case and a test.

In the code, the AI model only suggests the split of days between cities. Our own rules then check its answer, and if the model is down or gives a bad answer, a normal (non-AI) planner is used instead.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: A requirement is only useful if someone can check it against the build. So each requirement got an ID and a status, Done if it works in the current build and Planned if it is left for the final submission. This also made the gaps visible: the expense log (FR-25), the read-only share link (FR-26) and the time-to-complete measurement (FR-27) are still planned.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
• The requirements page (docs/requirements.md) has a Scope section that says plainly what changed from the proposal: AI is used for the city split only, it is checked by our own rules, and the app still works without it.
  • Requirements are grouped as in the course: functional (FR-1 to FR-27), non-functional product, organisational and external, and domain requirements (DR-1 to DR-5).
  • The same change is explained in the report under "Changes Since the Proposal".

docs.title: Data Model
docs.text:
The second task of the week was the ER diagram. I drew it in Chen notation with eight entities: User, Trip, City, Hotel, Trip Day, Activity, Budget and City Plan.

The question was which entities are weak. Hotel, Budget and City Plan have no key of their own, because each exists only as part of a city or a trip, so they are drawn as weak entities with identifying relationships.

A second question was how to show that a whole trip is stored as one Firestore document. I kept the ER diagram as the logical model and explained the storage separately in the data model page. A trip is small enough to stay well below Firestore's 1 MiB document limit, and it loads and saves in one read or write. The relationship between a trip and its days is partly redundant, since a day already points to its city, but I kept it because the days are stored directly under the trip.

docs.title: Week 2 : An Activity Diagram that Did Not Follow the Course Notation
Use Cases and the Activity Diagram
Problem
docs.text: My first activity diagram of the "Create a trip" use case looked correct, but when I compared it with the course slides on activity diagrams it did not follow the notation.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The use case diagram and the use case descriptions came first. There are twelve use cases: UC-1 to UC-7 come from the requirements, and UC-8 to UC-12 are supporting use cases that the main ones include or extend. For example, UC-2 Create a trip includes UC-8 Plan city split, and UC-9 Use fallback planner extends UC-8. Each use case is written with the template from the course.

The activity diagram describes UC-2, from the moment the traveller presses Generate to the moment the new roadmap opens.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Comparing my first version with the slides, these things were wrong:

  • Several arrows entered an action directly. The course notation uses a merge diamond for this, with several entries and one exit.
  • The exits of the decisions were not all labelled with guards in square brackets, which together must cover every case.
  • I had used dashed arrows, which are not part of the activity notation.
  • The swimlanes did not follow the rule that each action sits in the lane of the object that performs it.

I also found one factual mistake while checking the diagram against the code. I had an action for savings tips, but the code works them out when the trip page is shown, not when the trip is generated. The action became "Work out the budget (eight categories)".

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
I redrew the diagram with one start, end nodes, merge diamonds, decisions whose guards cover every case, and five swimlanes: Traveller, TripEase, AI provider, Places provider and Cloud Firestore. The four place searches for a city run at the same time in the code, but they are drawn as one action, so the diagram needs no fork and join.

Graphviz could not align swimlanes using clusters, so the layout is fixed by hand (neato -n). I then wrote a ten step walkthrough in docs/activity-diagram.md and checked every step against the code: the token check, the Zod validation, the single retry with a repair note, the fallback planner, the second check on the server, the feasibility rule for adding a stop to a day, the transfer on the first day of each new city, the budget and the save to Firestore.

docs.title: Week 3 : Unit Tests for the Formatting Helpers, and the Shared UI and Sign-in Screens
Problem
docs.text: The helpers in lib/utils.ts format money, durations and dates everywhere in the app, but they had no unit tests of their own.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text: There are six helpers: cn (joins class names), formatMoney, formatDurationShort, formatDateShort, formatDateLong and addDaysIso. formatMoney groups digits the Indian way, so one lakh is written as ₹1,00,000, and it falls back to the currency code for a currency it does not know. The date helpers work in UTC so that a date does not move by a day in another time zone.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: Most of the value was in the edge cases, not in the normal case: rounding of half values, zero and negative durations, a rollover across a month, a year or a leap day, and the same calendar day in any time zone.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: I wrote 26 tests in six groups with Vitest in utils.test.ts, one group for each helper. They check, for example, that formatMoney(1234567) gives ₹12,34,567, that formatDurationShort(-30) gives 0m, and that addDaysIso("2028-02-28", 1) gives 2028-02-29. All of them pass in continuous integration.

docs.title: Shared UI and Sign-in Screens
docs.text:
I also worked on the shared interface components and the sign-in screens.

  • Components. Button has five variants (primary, secondary, outline, danger, ghost) and four sizes. Chip is a toggle button that sets aria-pressed. Progress is the budget bar and keeps its value between 0 and 100. They all merge their classes with cn, and they support dark mode.
  • Sign-in and sign-up. The two pages are only a few lines each. Both use the same AuthForm with a mode value, so the form is written once. If the user had started a trip on the landing page, the form sends them back to the trip wizard after signing in, so what they typed is kept.
  • Auth state. Firebase Auth state exists only in the browser, so AuthProvider listens for it and keeps a loading flag until the first answer arrives. RequireAuth uses it to guard the protected pages: it shows a placeholder while the state is unknown and sends a visitor who is not signed in to the sign-in page, so the page does not flash first.

Roll No. 1024030712 Name: Manraj Singh

docs.title: Week 1 : Protecting the API Routes and the Data, and the Firebase Layer
Issue
docs.text: The API routes that call outside services (city planning, itinerary generation, place search) spend money and quota. Anyone who could call them could use up the project's Places and AI quota. At the same time the app has no separate backend, so the database itself had to protect each user's trips.

docs.title: Cause
docs.text:
• A route handler accepts any request unless it checks who is calling.
  • Firestore with default rules lets any client read and write.
  • The usual way to verify a Firebase login on a server is the Firebase Admin SDK. That needs a service-account private key, which is one more long-lived secret to keep safe, and an earlier key in this project had already ended up in the wrong file.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
1. Verify the ID token ourselves. A Firebase ID token is an RS256 JWT signed by Google. lib/server/firebase-auth.ts verifies it with jose against Google's public keys (createRemoteJWKSet, which caches the keys). It checks the issuer, the audience (our project id) and the algorithm. This needs no secret at all.

  • requireUser reads the Authorization: Bearer ... header on every route.
  • If the server is not configured, it fails closed with 500 and never lets the request through.
  • When a token is bad, the reply is always the same, "Invalid or expired session". The reason is hidden on purpose, because a detailed reason helps someone who is probing the endpoint.

2. Signed photo links. The browser loads place photos with <img src>, which cannot send a bearer header. Each photo link carries an HMAC signature that the server created, and /api/places/photo serves only links with a valid signature (compared with timingSafeEqual). The Places API key is added only on the server and never appears in a response.

3. Firestore rules that deny by default. A trip can be read only by its owner. On create the caller must write their own uid as ownerId, and ownerId cannot be changed later. Anything not matched is denied.

4. The browser side. lib/api-client.ts has one function, postAuthenticated, which every call to a protected route uses. It takes the current user's ID token from the Firebase SDK, which refreshes it when needed, and sends it in the Authorization header. The token is never stored or logged. If nobody is signed in, the call fails at once with a 401 message. A network failure and a failed reply each give a readable message, and the server's own error text is used when there is one.

5. One module for sign-in. lib/services/auth.ts is the only place that calls Firebase Auth (email sign-up and sign-in, Google sign-in, sign-out and the listener for the sign-in state). If the identity provider ever changes, only this file changes. authErrorMessage turns Firebase error codes (wrong password, existing email, closed popup, network error and so on) into messages for the user. An unknown code gives a generic message, and only in development the raw code is added so that a wrong configuration can be found.

6. Firebase set-up that survives a missing configuration. lib/firebase.ts reads the NEXT_PUBLIC_* values. If they are missing, for example in CI where there are no secrets, the Firebase SDK would throw while the pages are being prepared and the build would fail. So the file uses a placeholder configuration, and the browser console shows a clear error. A getApps() check stops a second initialisation when Next.js reloads the module during development. With NEXT_PUBLIC_USE_FIREBASE_EMULATOR=true the app connects to the local Auth and Firestore emulators, and only on the first initialisation, because connecting twice throws.

docs.title: Trade-off
docs.text: Without the Admin SDK the server cannot see that a token was revoked. A token of a signed-out or disabled account stays valid until it expires, which is at most one hour. For this app the threat is a stranger using up quota, so this window is acceptable. The code comment says that anything that needs instant revocation should move to the Admin SDK.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: The rules are tested with the Firestore emulator (11 tests in tests/rules/). The CI also has a separate job that scans the repository for secrets (gitleaks).

docs.title: Week 2 : An AI City Planner that Cannot Break the App
City Planning with Validation, One Retry and a Fallback
Issue
docs.text: The model suggests how many days to spend in each city. A model can return a valid-looking answer that is impossible, for example four cities with eleven days for a nine-day trip, or it can return broken JSON, time out or run out of quota. The traveller must never see a broken generation screen because of that.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
planCities follows one rule: the AI proposes, TripEase validates, and a deterministic planner catches everything else.

attempt -> Zod -> constraint checks -> (one repair retry) -> fallback
  • Provider seam. The planner depends only on the AIProvider interface. Groq and a mock provider implement it. A new vendor is a new class, and services/planning does not change.
  • Two layers of checks. Zod checks the shape of the answer. Then validateCityAllocation checks that the plan is possible: the days add up to the trip length, no city is repeated, every city has at least one day, there are at most 8 cities and not more cities than days. The destination must also match the one that was asked for.
  • One retry only. The retry happens for a plan that breaks a rule, or for malformed JSON or a wrong schema. It carries a repair note with the problems found, so it is a correction and not a new roll of the dice. Auth, quota and timeout errors are not retried, because a retry would only cost time and money.
  • Fallback. If there is no model configured, or the retry fails too, planCitiesDeterministically is used. The saved plan records its source (ai or fallback) and the reason.
  • No false claims. A mock provider does not reason, so its plans are recorded as fallback, not ai.

docs.title: The Fallback Planner
docs.text: For a curated destination (Thailand) it uses a known split of cities. It never gives a city fewer than two days, because each extra stop costs about half a day of travel. Without that rule a 3-day Thailand trip became "one night in Bangkok, then fly to Phuket". For any other destination it stays in one place. An earlier version split unknown places into names like " City" and " Coast", which looked real but were invented, so I removed it.

docs.title: The Groq Provider and the Plan Route
docs.text:
Groq provider. GroqAIProvider calls Groq's chat-completions endpoint with fetch. The model is openai/gpt-oss-120b unless GROQ_MODEL says otherwise, the temperature is 0.3 and a request is stopped after 20 seconds.

  • The request asks for json_schema output in strict mode with the planner's own schema. Not every model accepts a schema. If the server answers 400 and mentions the schema, the provider remembers this, writes a warning and tries once more in plain json_object mode. The answer is validated in the same way in both modes, so only the strength of the constraint is lost.
  • For a retry, the repair note is added as an extra message: "Your previous answer was rejected" followed by the problems found.
  • Every failure gets a code: timeout, provider-error (unreachable or any other status), auth (401 and 403), quota (429), malformed-json (not JSON or empty) and schema (JSON of the wrong shape). These codes decide whether the planner retries.
  • The error body from Groq is written to the server log only, cut to 300 characters. It is never sent to the browser, because it can contain parts of the prompt or hints about the key.

Choosing the provider. getAIProvider() is the only place that decides. AI_PROVIDER=groq with a GROQ_API_KEY gives Groq, mock gives the mock provider, and anything else returns nothing, so the deterministic planner is used. A missing key or an unknown value writes a warning. The key has no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix, so it stays on the server. aiProviderStatus() says whether AI is live without showing the key.

The route. POST /api/trips/plan first checks the user's token. Then it parses the body with tripDraftInputSchema, checks that the end date is not before the start date, counts the days and calls planCities. A failure gives a general message and status 500, and the details go to the log. The route is separate from /api/trips/generate so that the wizard can show the chosen cities as soon as they are ready, and does not pay for planning twice.

groq-provider.test.ts checks the schema request, the switch to JSON mode, the error codes, prose and wrong-shaped answers, the timeout and the repair note.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: planCities always returns a valid plan. If the fallback ever produced an invalid one, that is logged as an error instead of being shipped silently.

docs.title: Week 3 : A Feasibility Engine Built on Honest Estimates, and a Map that Never Guesses
Distance, Travel Time, the Clock and Map Points
Issue
docs.text: A generated day can look fine and still be impossible: too many stops, too far apart, no time to travel. The app needed a way to tell the traveller that a day is too full, without calling a paid routing service.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Distance is calculated locally. geo.ts uses the haversine formula for the great-circle distance. No provider call is made, which matters when the Places quota is small. A coordinate is valid only if it is a finite number in range and is not (0, 0), because (0, 0) is nearly always a provider default meaning "unknown". If a distance cannot be worked out, the result is null, and a guessed distance is never used instead.

Travel time is a heuristic. travel-time.ts turns a straight-line distance into a journey:

  • Distances are multiplied by 1.3 for roads (flights are not).
  • Inside a city: walking up to 1.2 km, then car in bands of speed.
  • Between cities: car up to 120 km, train up to 400 km, flight beyond that. Every mode has a fixed overhead, so a flight includes the 180 minutes of getting to and from the airport.
  • Every result is marked isEstimated: true, so the screen can say "estimated". The code sits behind a TravelTimeProvider interface, so a real routing service could replace it later.

Durations. A duration given by a provider is used when there is one. Otherwise the engine uses a middle value for the category (for example 90 minutes for sightseeing and 75 for food). The model is never asked to invent a duration.

Opening hours. The Places integration does not request opening hours, because they are a separate billable field. The check therefore answers "unknown", and missing hours are not an error. When the field is turned on later, only the provider needs to change.

Map points. The same rule, unknown stays unknown, is used for the map. map-points.ts turns a saved trip into a flat list of points.

  • A hotel or an activity becomes a point only if it has a coordinate. A place without one is not drawn, and no pin is put at a guessed position. countUnmappablePlaces counts the missing ones, so the screen can say how many.
  • A point has the id of its activity, or hotel:<cityId> for a hotel. The roadmap and the map use this one key, and roadmapElementId is the single place that turns it into a page element id, so the two cannot drift apart.
  • filterMapPoints has three modes: all, one city, or one day. In day mode the hotel of the city stays visible, because the day starts and ends there.
  • routeForDay gives the points of a day in the planned order, and cityTransferLines gives straight lines between cities (the hotel is the anchor, or else the first mapped stop). Both are only "the order planned" and "these cities connect". They are not routes, because no routing service is used. For the day line the screen says: "Dashed line shows the order you planned this day — not a driving route."
  • Each point carries what its card shows (time, duration, rating, address, link and source name), copied from the trip and never looked up. A duration of zero is treated as no duration, and a price counts as an estimate unless it is marked as exact.

map-points.test.ts covers these rules.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: The same arithmetic is used when a day is generated and when it is shown, so the generator does not create days that the engine would then mark red. A day is judged against the 09:00 to 21:00 window, 720 minutes. On the map, only places with a real coordinate are drawn.

docs.title: Week 4 : Places, Itineraries, API Routes, Saving Trips, the Budget Engine and CI
Places, Itinerary, Routes, Saving, Budget and CI
Places provider and cache
docs.text:
Issue. Generating a trip needs several searches for every city, and each one is a billable Google call. The app also has to work when there is no key.

Fix.

  • getPlacesProvider() is the only place where a provider is chosen. With PLACES_PROVIDER=google and a key it uses Google Places. In every other case, including a missing key (a warning is logged), it uses an offline mock provider. Everything else depends only on the PlacesProvider interface.
  • A search that fails or comes back empty falls back to the mock provider for that search only.
  • TtlCache is a small in-memory cache: entries live 10 minutes and there are at most 500, and the oldest unused one is dropped first. It is per server process on purpose. The worst case after a restart is a repeated call.

docs.title: Itinerary generator
docs.text: For each city it runs four searches at the same time with Promise.all: 1 hotel, 14 attractions, 12 restaurants and 4 nightlife places. Attractions are grouped by area so that each day covers one part of the city, and the stops are ordered nearest first. A stop is added to a day only if the day still fits in the available minutes, with time kept for dinner. The output is validated with a Zod schema before it is returned.

docs.title: Budget engine
docs.text:
budget-engine.ts is made of pure functions, so the screen can call them after every edit.

  • Eight categories: flights, hotels, food, activities, transport, shopping, miscellaneous and a buffer. Activities go into the category that matches them, hotels are the nightly price times the nights, and a fixed daily amount is added for local transport.
  • Miscellaneous is 4% of the other costs. The buffer is 5% of the user's budget, with a minimum of 3,000.
  • When the estimate is above the budget, buildSavingsSuggestions gives up to three rules-based suggestions: a cheaper hotel in the most expensive city (30% off), a shared tour instead of the most expensive non-food activity above 1,500 (60% off), and local restaurants instead of hotel dining (15% of the food cost). There is no model in this step, so every suggestion can be explained.

docs.title: API routes
docs.text:
The routes that spend quota (plan, generate, rebuild and places search) check the user's token first, and none of them sends the error text of an upstream provider to the browser. The plan route is described in Week 2.

  • /api/trips/generate. It validates the trip details, then accepts the city plan that the wizard already has. A plan sent by the browser is client input, so it is checked again with the same rules. If it is missing or not valid, the server plans again, so an old plan cannot block the user. The itinerary is checked with generatedItinerarySchema before it is returned, and a bad result gives a 502.
  • /api/trips/rebuild. It applies an edited city list. The request must have the trip details, 1 to 12 cities and the existing cities and days. The new allocation passes through validateCityAllocation, the check used for the AI plan. These are the traveller's own edits, so the exact problems are returned with status 400. The generator then receives the existing itinerary. A city that is still present, matched by name without regard to capital letters, keeps its hotel and its edited activities, and only a new city or an extra day causes a places search. A renamed city counts as new. places-request-count.test.ts checks that an unchanged rebuild makes no search. The saved plan is recorded as fallback with the reason "Cities edited by the traveller."
  • /api/places/search. It backs the "replace with a real place" box. If the live provider fails, or returns nothing, the route returns demo places and a short notice. The notice comes from friendlyPlacesMessage, which maps each error code (missing-key, invalid-key, quota-exceeded, network, malformed-response, provider-error) to a safe sentence, because a raw Google error can contain project ids and key hints. An HTTP 400, 401 or 403 from the provider is treated as an invalid key and a 429 as a quota problem. Every place is checked with placeSchema before it leaves the server, so a mapping bug in a provider fails here and does not reach a saved trip.

docs.title: Saving and editing a trip
docs.text:
trips.ts. It is the only file that touches Firestore for trip data. Components call its functions and never build queries.

  • A converter fills defaults when a field is missing (status "ready", currency INR, one traveller, solo) and turns timestamps into dates.
  • saveGeneratedTrip writes one document with the current user as ownerId. From the planning step it stores only the structured decision (the cities, the source and the reason), never the prompt or the raw model output.
  • subscribeToOwnerTrips and subscribeToTrip give live updates and return a function to stop listening. The trip list is filtered by owner and sorted by creation time, which needs a composite index. It is defined in firestore.indexes.json.
  • updateTripItinerary replaces the cities, days, budget or planning record in a single write.

trip-mutations.ts. These are pure functions, with no Firestore and no React. Adding, editing, deleting and reordering an activity, changing a hotel and applying a suggestion each return the new days or cities together with a budget recalculated by computeBudgetBreakdown. The flight cost already in the budget is kept. The three suggestions are applied with the same percentages that they were priced with: the hotel gets 70% of its price (30% off), the chosen activity 40% of its cost (60% off), and every food item 85% of its cost. The first two are marked as demo data and as estimates, and their old link, rating, image and source are removed, because they no longer describe a real place.

docs.title: CI and Deployment
docs.text:
The workflow ci.yml runs on every push and pull request. It installs Node 22 and Java 21 (the Firestore emulator needs Java), and then runs lint, the unit tests, the Firestore rules tests and a production build. A second job scans the repository for secrets.

The Firestore rules and indexes are published with npx firebase deploy --only firestore, and firebase.json defines the local emulators (Auth on port 9099, Firestore on 8085). Merges to main are deployed to a staging environment on Vercel. The Vercel project uses code/ as its root directory, and the six NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_* variables are set for Production and Preview. The Places and AI keys are optional: without them the mock providers are used and the app still works.

docs.title: Vatsal’s Journal
docs.text:
Roll No. 1024030714 Name: Vatsal Chauhan

  • W1 : The landing page, and keeping a visitor's trip idea alive through sign-up
